performers: Mary Garden, soprano; Claude Debussy, piano
intro: “Il pleure dans mon cœur” is the second of Debussy’s Ariettes oubliées, a setting of Verlaine. Mary Garden sings it with Debussy at the piano, in a recording made in Paris in 1904.

sections.label: A · Piano semiquavers under long vocal notes
sections.mNote: Long vocal notes held above running semiquavers in the piano.

sections.label: B · Piano chords under freer vocal line
sections.mNote: The piano changes to chords; the vocal line moves more freely.

sections.label: A′ · Last stanza over returning semiquavers
sections.mNote: The piano’s semiquavers return and continue after the voice stops.

cues.title: Piano semiquavers and vocal line
cues.text: The piano plays running semiquavers beneath the song. Over them the voice moves in longer notes, marked triste et monotone (sad and monotonous).
cues.evidence: Debussy, Ariettes oubliées, no. 2, voice-and-piano score, printed pp. 12–13: pp, con sordine, running semiquavers and the vocal marking triste et monotone. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/8/83/IMSLP14819-Debussy_-_Ariettes_oubli%C3%A9es_%28voice_and_piano%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Verlaine’s poem, 1874
cues.text: Verlaine’s rain falls on the roofs and the ground, and the speaker grieves without knowing why. There is no betrayal, and neither love nor hatred accounts for the pain. The poem appeared in Romances sans paroles in 1874, and in Debussy’s setting the vocal phrases recur.
cues.evidence: Paul Verlaine, Il pleure dans mon cœur, Romances sans paroles (1874), all four stanzas. French text: https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/853446.html. Recurrent vocal phrases are visible in the song score, pp. 12–17.

cues.title: Return of the opening tempo
cues.text: After the freer question about betrayal, marked Modéré, the piano’s running notes return at 1° Tempo. The final stanza names the worst pain as not knowing why the heart aches. The voice slows at Molto rallentando and ends, and the piano continues alone in a postlude.
cues.evidence: Voice-and-piano score, pp. 15–17: Modéré question, Revenez au 1er Mouvement, final stanza at 1° Tempo, Molto rallentando and piano postlude.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The semiquavers stop for the voice
transitions.from: A · Piano semiquavers under long vocal notes
transitions.to: B · Piano chords under freer vocal line
transitions.how: The piano’s running semiquavers stop. Debussy cancels the four-sharp key signature and marks the passage Modéré. The voice moves freely over chords and a short piano reply, and the score marks it ad libitum. At this point the poem asks whether betrayal explains the grief, in the question beginning Quoi! nulle trahison? (printed score, pp. 15–16).
transitions.evidence: Voice-and-piano score, printed pp. 15–16: cancelled key signature, Modéré, ad libitum and the question beginning Quoi! nulle trahison?

transitions.title: Semiquavers return for the last stanza
transitions.from: B · Piano chords under freer vocal line
transitions.to: A′ · Last stanza over returning semiquavers
transitions.how: The piano resumes its semiquavers while the voice holds the end of the word raison. Revenez au 1er Mouvement restores the opening tempo, and the four-sharp signature returns with the final stanza. The voice again sustains long notes above the semiquaver figure in the piano.
transitions.evidence: Voice-and-piano score, printed p. 16: semiquavers beneath the held vocal note, Revenez au 1er Mouvement and restored four-sharp signature at 1° Tempo.

source.title: Debussy, Ariettes oubliées no.2 · voice-and-piano score
source.locator: No. 2, printed pp. 12–17: running piano semiquavers, the freer central question and the piano postlude.

timeline.note: The voice holds long notes above running semiquavers in the piano.
The voice asks about betrayal; the piano’s semiquavers stop.
Running semiquavers return beneath the final stanza.
The piano continues the rain figure after the voice stops.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
